intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal recessive dilated cardiomyopathy-2A (CMD2A) is caused by homozygous mutation in the TNNI3 gene, which encodes cardiac troponin I.

checks.claim: Autosomal recessive dilated cardiomyopathy-2A (CMD2A) is caused by homozygous mutation in the TNNI3 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: TNNI3 is the first recessive gene identified for this condition, and we suggest that other such genes could be pinpointed by mutation analyses designed to identify homozygous mutations.
checks.explanation: Abstract establishes TNNI3 as a recessive DCM gene and implies homozygous mutation, but does not name CMD2A or explicitly state homozygosity.

checks.claim: The TNNI3 gene encodes cardiac troponin I.
checks.evidence_quote: the sarcomeric gene for cardiac troponin I (TNNI3)

paragraphs.text: Familial isolated idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy is usually inherited as an autosomal dominant trait with variable penetrance and expressivity. CMD2A is an autosomal recessive form of the disorder (Goldblatt et al., 1987). Murphy et al. (2004) identified the cardiac troponin I gene TNNI3 as the first gene for recessive idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy.

checks.claim: Familial isolated idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy is usually inherited as an autosomal dominant trait with variable penetrance and expressivity.
checks.evidence_quote: Familial, isolated, dilated cardiomyopathy is usually reported as being inherited in an autosomal dominant mode with variable penetrance and expressivity.
checks.explanation: The abstract says this almost word for word.

checks.claim: CMD2A is an autosomal recessive form of idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy.
checks.evidence_quote: In this paper we describe a form of autosomal recessively inherited, dilated, cardiomyopathy occurring in three members of a consanguineous Madeira Portuguese family.
checks.explanation: The paper describes an autosomal recessive form of idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy. The label 'CMD2A' is OMIM's own, and a later citing paper calls this the CMD2A phenotype originally described by Goldblatt et al.

checks.claim: Murphy et al. (2004) identified the cardiac troponin I gene TNNI3 as the first gene for recessive idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy.

paragraphs.text: Seliem et al. (2000) studied 55 consecutive patients younger than 10 years with dilated cardiomyopathy, seen over a 5-year period in the Eastern Province of Saudi Arabia. Echocardiography was the main diagnostic method. The 55 patients made up 20% of the offspring of 41 families of Arab descent. In 19 families (46%) the parents were first cousins, and in 22 families (54%) there was no obvious consanguinity. In 95% of patients, age at presentation was under 30 months (range, 1 to 100 months). Of the patients, 38% were male and 62% were female. Twenty-five patients (46%) died, 15 (27%) improved, and 15 (27%) recovered. At diagnosis, the left ventricular shortening fraction ranged from 5 to 28%, and it did not differ among those who died, improved, or recovered.

paragraphs.text: Goldblatt et al. (1987) reported autosomal recessive inheritance of idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy in a consanguineous Madeira Portuguese family. In infants of Arab descent from Saudi Arabia, Seliem et al. (2000) performed complex segregation analysis using the mixed model of inheritance and found that a recessive model fit the family data best. In the family studied by Murphy et al. (2004), the disease was recessive.

paragraphs.text: Carballo et al. (2009) found 2 heterozygous missense TNNI3 mutations, lys36-to-gln (K36Q) and asn185-to-lys (N185K), in a panel of 96 probands with dilated cardiomyopathy. Each mutation was associated with severe, early-onset familial dilated cardiomyopathy. These were the first reported autosomal dominant mutations in TNNI3 causing dilated cardiomyopathy.

paragraphs.text: Murphy et al. (2004) analyzed the TNNI3 gene in 235 patients with dilated cardiomyopathy, using a method able to detect both dominant and recessive mutations. In a family with recessive disease, they found a novel TNNI3 mutation. In functional studies, the mutation impaired troponin interactions, which could reduce myocardial contractility.
